title: My hair was black
hook: Ambapali's song of her aging body: once lovely, now changed; the truth's word never fails (Therigatha, Ambapali)
carry: so it was, so it is

segments.voice: Yesterday, kalyanamitta: Kisa Gotami's song put good friends first, before grief. Your line was good friends. This week the sisters sang of a nun who finally stayed, a flame gone out, washed feet, grieving mothers, a foster mother's thanks, and good friends. Today, a woman looks at her own body across the years.

Black as bees, curled at the tips. That's how Ambapali remembers her hair. The path met her before as the courtesan of Vesali who hosted the Buddha for a meal and gave his community her mango grove. In the Therigatha she is an old nun, and her song walks down her own body, from her hair to her feet, then and now. Every verse ends the same way.
screen: `BLACK AS BEES.` → `A COURTESAN, THEN A NUN.` → `ONE REFRAIN, EVERY VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, then and now. My hair was black, she says, the color of bees, curled at the tips. Now, with age, it's like coarse bark fiber. Then the refrain: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth. So it was; so it is. Second, the walk. She goes on, part by part. Eyes that shone like jewels, now dim. A voice sweet as a cuckoo's in the forest, now faltering. Teeth once bright, now broken. Each verse holds a then and a now, and each closes with the same line; the repeating is part of the teaching. Third, who is speaking. This is the woman who, in the sutta of the Buddha's last journey, wouldn't give up a meal with him for all of Vesali, and then gave his community her grove. A woman who knew what beauty and wealth could buy tells us, steadily, what time did. Fourth, the tone. Some readers hear grief in the song. Others hear something calmer: no complaint, no shame, only accuracy. Near the end she says this body is like an old house with its plaster falling away. And the refrain says the Buddha's word holds: things change. In her mouth that isn't a curse. It's a teaching confirmed, by her own skin.
screen: `BLACK HAIR, NOW LIKE BARK.` · `EYES, VOICE, TEETH: THEN AND NOW.` · `ONCE THE COURTESAN OF VESALI.` · `AN OLD HOUSE, PLASTER FALLING.` · then, large: `SO IT WAS, SO IT IS.`

segments.voice: Find one old photograph of yourself, on your phone, in a drawer, or from memory, and look at it the way Ambapali looked at herself: hair then, face then, and softly, so it was. Then feel the body you're in right now, breathing and here, and let so it is sit beside it, with nothing to argue and nothing to praise.
Sacca. Truth: the word behind Ambapali's refrain, that the truth-speaker's word holds, as her song walks her own body, then and now. Today's word.
Your line: so it was, so it is. No complaint, no shame, just what time did. That's day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Reflection on the body's changes is a traditional Buddhist contemplation, and Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada settings as a picture of impermanence seen in one's own body.

chat.says: Is Ambapali's poem about growing old just a sad complaint?
options: Some hear grief, but she names each change plainly, the truth confirmed.
Yes. She's bitter that becoming a nun took her beauty away.
No. She says her body never changed, thanks to her practice.
chat.meaning: Ambapali walks her body, then and now, and each verse ends: the truth-speaker's word holds. Some hear grief; others hear calm accuracy, no complaint.
